name: Bariatric body contouring

lead: After large weight loss, often following bariatric surgery, many people are left with hanging skin around the belly, arms, thighs, buttocks and breasts. Body contouring is the set of operations that removes that skin and tightens the shape underneath.

The payoff is a smoother, more defined silhouette that fits clothes better and matches the weight lost. Surgical reviews describe a wide range of operations, and studies measure both complications and patient-reported body satisfaction.

paras: Procedures commonly include abdominoplasty or belt lipectomy for the trunk, brachioplasty for the arms, thigh lifts and breast or chest reshaping, often staged over several operations once weight has stabilised. Surgeons also assess nutrition, since protein and iron status affect healing.

Reported risks include wound-healing problems, seroma, infection, scarring, blood clots and anaemia. Studies link complications to smoking and higher pre-operative BMI. Reviews of arm lifts report complications in roughly 29 percent of patients across 27 studies.

chain: Smoother silhouette matching the lower weight
angle.text: The surgery removes the skin and tissue that large weight loss leaves behind, changing outline and how clothes sit. It is the main route for people whose skin does not retract.

lead: Bariatric or post-bariatric body contouring is the group of plastic surgery procedures that remove excess skin and reshape the body after major weight loss. It addresses the abdomen, arms, buttocks, thighs and breasts, and demand has risen alongside bariatric surgery.[1][2][3]

For appearance, it converts weight loss into a visible change in shape: excess tissue that diet and exercise cannot reduce is removed, and the trunk and limbs are tightened. Wikipedia notes that changes after contouring emerge gradually over years.[4] Typical operations include abdominoplasty (tummy tuck), including circumferential belt lipectomy or lower body lift, and arm lifts.[5][6]

Research consists mainly of surgical case series, literature reviews and a few trials that look at complications, nutrition, wound care and patient-reported quality of life, such as the Body-QoL instrument developed for aesthetic and post-bariatric patients.[1][7][8]
infobox: Abdominoplasty, belt lipectomy, brachioplasty, thigh lift
After major weight loss or bariatric surgery

paras: A review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal describes anatomical deformities in each region after massive weight loss, with surgical options for each, and stresses that the problem is not solely surgical because nutritional and psychological factors matter.[1] Abdominoplasty variants include complete, mini, extended and circumferential forms; the circumferential belt lipectomy is commonly used after massive weight loss to contour abdomen, flanks and lower back.[6]

A literature review of brachioplasty found 27 studies from 1995 to 2015 covering 1,065 patients, with complications in 308 (28.9 percent).[5] An Italian series of 78 ex-obese patients operated between 2007 and 2016 found adverse events related to cigarette smoking and pre-operative BMI, and described a management protocol.[9]

A Brazilian randomised trial compared intravenous with oral iron for anaemia after post-bariatric abdominoplasty, noting reduced oral iron absorption after bariatric surgery.[10] A study of protein supplementation in massive-weight-loss patients having abdominoplasty examined wound-healing complications.[11] A retrospective analysis addressed venous thromboembolism risk in massive-weight-loss body contouring.[12] Newer reviews and clinical trial registrations cover abdominoplasty outcomes, nutrition and quality of life.[13]

Abdominoplasty generally has a higher complication rate than many cosmetic operations, including seroma, hematoma, infection, delayed healing, necrosis, scarring, sensation changes and clots; smoking, obesity and diabetes raise risk.[6] Post-bariatric patients may also face nutritional deficiencies affecting healing.[1][11]
